strengths: The paper tackles a relevant problem (inference-time steering for LLMs and VLMs) and proposes a unified framework that works across both modalities without retraining or external modules, which is a practically useful contribution.

The evaluation breadth is good: two LLMs and three VLMs, spanning TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, and SPA-VL, with additional checks on MMLU/MMMU to verify that general capabilities are preserved.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: comparison of attribution methods (IG vs. SmoothGrad vs. vanilla gradients vs. random selection), token count k, steering strength alpha, modality-specific variants (vision-only/text-only), and the preference-based attribution objective.
The analysis of side effects is a valuable aspect: showing that CAA severely degrades MMLU/MMMU while GRAINS preserves reasoning is an informative finding about existing steering methods.
Runtime/cost reporting (96s for LLM, 302s for VLM steering vector construction) and comparison to LoRA fine-tuning costs help position the method's practicality.
Figure 3's ablation of top attributed tokens provides evidence that the attribution signal is meaningfully directional (removing negative-attribution tokens shifts preference toward y_pos).
weaknesses: There is a mismatch between the narrative and the actual mechanism: the paper claims fine-grained, token-level, input-sensitive interventions, but at inference time the same steering vector is added uniformly to every position and layer (Eq. 7). The token selectivity only enters during steering vector construction, so the claimed 'targeted, proportional' intervention is overclaimed.

Key implementation details needed for reproduction are missing or unclear: which layers are steered (and how they are selected) is never specified; the code footnote is empty; and the baseline hyperparameter search protocol is described only at a high level.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite gains on some benchmarks being small (e.g., FaithEval +2.94 over base, Gemma MMMU -0.72, MMHal 0.473 vs. LoRA 0.461 on Qwen where the method is actually worse than LoRA).
There is an internal inconsistency: the Base Model Toxigen accuracy is 51.19 in Table 1 but 48.10 in Table 6 for Llama-3.1-8B, which undermines confidence in the reported numbers.

The novelty is moderate: the method combines well-known components (Integrated Gradients for token attribution, contrastive activation differences as in ITI/CAA, PCA aggregation as in ICV) into a pipeline; the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new versus re-engineered.

Some evaluation protocols are weak or under-specified: TruthfulQA evaluation variant (mc1/mc2) and the 'BLEU accuracy' metric are not precisely defined; MMHal-Bench hallucination rate judging procedure is not described; SPA-VL 'chosen > rejected' log-likelihood is a proxy metric rather than measuring actual generation safety.

The method requires preference pairs (y_pos, y_neg) and 50 task-specific examples per behavior, making it task-specific in practice; the paper's framing of 'model-agnostic, no supervision' downplays this requirement, and the ablation showing a single reference output works is only briefly covered.

Writing has multiple typos and editorial slips ('constructs constructs', 'An another attribution methods', footnote lambda vs. alpha symbol mismatch, stray parenthesis), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully polished.
Excluding ITI and RepE baselines based on a citation is defensible but weakens completeness; and adapted CAA for VLMs may not represent a strong multimodal baseline.

strengths: The core idea — using contrastive Integrated Gradients attribution to select influential tokens before constructing steering vectors — is a reasonable and somewhat novel integration of interpretability tooling into activation steering, and the paper is upfront that the contribution is the pipeline rather than a new attribution method.

Coverage is broad: five models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) across five benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), with side evaluations of general capabilities (MMLU/MMMU) and BLEU-based generation quality, which is the right set of checks for a steering method.

Ablations are appropriately targeted: attribution method (IG vs. SmoothGrad vs. vanilla vs. random), modality-specific vs. joint attribution, and preference-based vs. likelihood-based objective each isolate a claimed design choice, and all support the design decisions.

The ablation experiment in Fig. 3 (ablating negatively-attributed tokens increases preference for the aligned response, and vice versa) provides a direct sanity check that the IG signal is behaviorally meaningful, not merely correlational.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (steering strength α and token count k) is analyzed in the appendix on a held-out dev set, and the runtime cost of vector construction is reported, which helps practical assessment.
weaknesses: No statistical rigor: there are no error bars, confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests anywhere. Many margins over baselines are small (e.g., Toxigen Llama 60.98 vs. ICV 59.07; FaithEval Qwen 64.77 vs. LoRA 64.96 — GRAINS actually loses to LoRA there; Gemma-3-12B hallucination 0.442 vs. ICT 0.457), and with only 50 steering samples the results could be fragile.

Internal inconsistency undermines confidence: the base-model Toxigen accuracy for Llama-3.1-8B is 51.19 in Table 1 but 48.10 in Table 6, with no explanation. Such discrepancies in headline numbers require careful auditing.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the code footnote (footnote 1) is literally empty in the manuscript. Given that the method involves many undisclosed implementation choices (IG baseline construction, masking semantics for visual patches, which layers are steered and how layer vectors are combined, the number of PCA components, tokenization of masked patch positions), this makes independent verification essentially impossible as submitted.

The gains over the strongest steering baselines are modest and uneven. On TruthfulQA, CAA reaches 44.62 vs. GRAINS 47.37 on Llama (and the abstract's '13.22% gain' is against the base model, not the best baseline). On Qwen2.5-VL MMHal, LoRA (0.461) beats GRAINS (0.473). The framing 'consistently outperforms fine-tuning' overstates what the tables show.

Causal language is stronger than the evidence: the paper claims to identify tokens with 'the greatest causal influence' and to intervene 'precisely on the dimensions responsible for misalignment,' but IG attribution is a saliency heuristic; the ablation in Fig. 3 supports directional signal, yet no analysis shows the steering vector's effect is actually mediated by the selected tokens rather than by the generic PCA-of-activation-differences step (which resembles ICV/CAA and might work nearly as well without attribution — a missing ablation that isolates the attribution's contribution at inference time, not just at token-selection time).

The evaluation protocol has leakage/selection concerns: steering vectors are built from 50 samples of the target datasets and evaluated on held-out splits of the same distribution and the same prompts templates; there is no evidence of cross-dataset generalization (e.g., steering on TruthfulQA and testing on FaithEval), which would substantiate the 'generalizable behavior direction' claim.

Only two or three models per setting and a single 10/90 split; combined with dev-set hyperparameter selection for GRAINS (α tuned per model) vs. original-paper hyperparameters for baselines, the comparison could favor the proposed method.

Writing quality is below acceptance standard: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('Qwen2.5-7B-Intruct', 'constructs constructs', 'there are other steering baselines ... Noted that', a stray closing parenthesis in the abstract-adjacent paragraph), an undefined 'BLEU accuracy' metric that is non-standard and needs a clearer definition, and inconsistent notation (α vs. λ for steering strength between Eq. 7 and Appendix A.2).

The preference-based loss requires paired preferred/dispreferred outputs per input; for toxicity/truthfulness settings the provenance of these pairs for the 50 steering samples is not fully specified, raising questions about how comparable the setup is to baselines that do not consume such supervision.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant gap in the inference-time steering literature: most existing methods (CAA, ITI, ICV) apply uniform, globally-derived interventions, and the proposal to use contrastive Integrated Gradients to identify causally influential tokens (across both visual and textual modalities) before constructing steering vectors is a sensible and well-motivated idea.

The method is presented clearly, with a well-structured three-stage pipeline (attribution, contrastive vector construction via PCA, normalized additive steering at inference), and the theoretical justification for choosing IG over vanilla gradients and SmoothGrad is sound.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 2 LLMs and 3 VLMs, across truthfulness (TruthfulQA), toxicity (Toxigen), faithfulness (FaithEval), hallucination (MMHal-Bench), and safety preference (SPA-VL), with comparisons to both PEFT (LoRA) and multiple steering baselines (ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT).

The analysis of collateral damage is a valuable addition: showing that GRAINS preserves MMLU/MMMU performance while baselines like CAA degrade it substantially (e.g., CAA drops Llama-3.1-8B MMLU by ~17.8%) directly supports the paper's central claim that selective intervention avoids overcorrection.

The paper includes multiple useful ablations (attribution method, token count k, steering strength α, modality-only variants, preference vs. likelihood objective), including a random-selection lower bound, and Figure 3 provides a sanity check that ablations of positively/negatively attributed tokens move the preference margin in the expected directions.
Qualitative examples (Fig. 4, Fig. 7) illustrate both correction of hallucinations and preservation of correct base-model behavior, which supports the 'no regression' claim.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete: the code footnote ('Code:') is empty. Several methodological details needed for reproduction are missing or underspecified, e.g., which layers are steered (the paper says 'across layers' but never states which layers or how they are chosen), how the IG baseline embedding is instantiated for visual patches, and how the hallucination rate on MMHal-Bench is judged (human, GPT-judge, or automatic metric).

There are numerical inconsistencies across tables that undermine confidence: the Toxigen base accuracy for Llama-3.1-8B is 51.19 in Table 1 but 48.10 in Table 6; and the appendix states performance peaks at k=3 for Llama and k=5 for Qwen, while Section 4.1 asserts k=3 'in all experiments.' These need reconciliation.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, despite evaluation subsets that may be small (e.g., 10/90 dev/test splits of a limited pool, 50 steering samples). Given that some margins over baselines are modest (e.g., FaithEval on Qwen where LoRA at 64.96 actually beats GRAINS at 64.77), variance reporting is necessary to support the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

The framing slightly oversells token-specificity: at inference time (Eq. 7) the steering vector is added uniformly to every token position at a layer, exactly like the global-vector baselines the paper criticizes. Token attribution only influences vector construction offline; the intervention itself is not input- or token-sensitive, which weakens the claimed distinction from prior fixed-vector methods.

The LoRA baseline appears weak: it is fine-tuned for only 10 iterations on the same 50 steering samples, which makes the 'outperforms fine-tuning' headline claim less convincing than it sounds; a better-tuned PEFT baseline would strengthen the comparison.

Dataset-specific steering vectors are constructed from 50 samples per dataset/task, so the method is per-task and per-attribute; the paper does not discuss cross-domain transfer or how many samples are minimally needed, which limits claims of practical generality.

Evaluation metric choices are not fully specified: TruthfulQA 'accuracy' (MC1? MC2?) and the BLEU-accuracy metric for generation quality are nonstandard or underdefined, making results hard to compare to the literature.

Some writing issues remain (e.g., 'Qwen2.5-7B-Intruct', 'construct constructs', inconsistent notation α vs. λ for steering strength between Eq. 7 and Appendix A.2), and the hyperparameter-selection protocol (tuning on dev sets for baselines but a separate analysis for GRAINS) should be stated more uniformly.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: using contrastive Integrated Gradients to identify the most influential tokens (across both visual and textual modalities) and building directional steering vectors from contrastive activations, unifying LLM and VLM steering without external modules, token sampling, or retraining.

The experimental coverage is broad and mostly convincing: 2 LLMs and 3 VLMs, three safety-critical LLM benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval), two multimodal benchmarks (MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), plus capability-preservation checks (MMLU, MMMU), cross-dataset generalization (RTP, POPE), and a 72B-scale result.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough and directly support the design choices: IG vs. vanilla gradients/SmoothGrad/random selection (Table 8), PC1 vs. mean aggregation (Table 9), last-token vs. all-token injection (Table 10), modality-specific vs. joint attribution (Tables 12-13), preference vs. likelihood objective (Table 14), and norm preservation (Table 15).

Inference-time overhead is well characterized (~3.5% throughput drop, one-time 96-302s vector construction), and the norm-preserving formulation in Eq. 5 is a sensible mechanism for avoiding capability degradation.
Writing and figures (Figs. 1-2) are clear; hyperparameter sensitivity (lambda, k) and failure modes (undercorrection) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is limited: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and several evaluation sets are small (e.g., MMHal-Bench has only 96 questions; steering vectors are built from just 50 samples). Differences such as 0.476 vs. 0.497 average hallucination rate may not be meaningful without variance estimates.
The footnote 'Code:' is empty - no code or artifact link is actually provided, weakening reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

Novelty is moderate: the method combines established components (Integrated Gradients for attribution, contrastive activation differences in the spirit of CAA, PCA-based vector extraction as in ITI-style approaches). The main novelty is the attribution-guided, token-targeted formulation and its application to VLMs, which is valuable but incremental.

Steering vectors are constructed from 50 samples of a dataset and evaluated on the test split of the same dataset; while Section 5.3 tests cross-dataset transfer, the main-table gains partly benefit from in-distribution vector construction, and baselines tuned on the same data narrow the apparent advantage.
The exclusion of RepE and ITI baselines is justified only by citing other papers' results rather than direct comparison under the authors' setup, which weakens baseline completeness.

Several metrics are loosely specified in the main text (e.g., 'multiple-choice accuracy' for Toxigen and FaithEval, SPA-VL log-likelihood win rate), and the GPT-4o judge validation for MMHal rests on only 9 human annotations.

Some claims are imprecise: the abstract reports '13.22%' TruthfulQA improvement where the table shows an absolute gain of 13.22 points from 34.15 to 47.37; relative-vs-absolute reporting should be clarified.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem—making inference-time steering more targeted and interpretable—and the idea of using contrastive Integrated Gradients over a preference-based objective to select influential tokens is a sensible bridge between attribution methods and activation steering, unifying LLM and VLM settings.

The evaluation is broad: two LLMs and three VLMs across truthfulness, toxicity, faithfulness, hallucination, and safety benchmarks, with comparisons to multiple recent steering baselines (ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT, RUDDER, SHARP) as well as LoRA fine-tuning.

There is a reasonably extensive ablation suite: attribution method (IG vs. SmoothGrad vs. vanilla gradients vs. random), PCA vs. mean aggregation, token count k, steering strength λ, layer-wise vs. last-token injection, modality-specific vs. joint attribution, and the normalization step.

The paper reports computational overhead (IG construction time, <5% inference throughput drop), cross-dataset generalization (Toxigen→RTP, MMHal→POPE), and a scale experiment on Qwen2.5-VL-72B, which strengthens the empirical picture.
Writing and figures are generally clear; the method (Sec. 3) is described in enough detail to follow, and hyperparameter ranges and sample-construction procedures are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars anywhere. Several headline margins are small (e.g., 0.514 vs. 0.461 on MMHal for Qwen-VL; 59.76 vs. 59.65 average over CAA for Llama), and with the small evaluation sets used (e.g., 500 subsampled SPA-VL test samples for the 72B experiment; MMHal-Bench is small), many claimed gains may not be statistically meaningful.

The SPA-VL evaluation metric—preference win rate computed from model log-likelihoods of chosen vs. rejected responses—is potentially circular for steering methods. Since GRAINS explicitly constructs its steering vector to increase log P(y_pos) relative to log P(y_neg) (Eq. 1), reporting win rates measured by the same quantity risks rewarding methods for exactly what they optimize, rather than for genuinely better generations. GPT-4o-judged or human evaluation on free-form SPA-VL generations would be needed to support the alignment claims.

Multiple-choice accuracy on TruthfulQA (mc1) is a noisy and heavily saturated-by-hacks metric; headline claims like '+13.22% TruthfulQA accuracy' rest largely on it, and no open-ended TruthfulQA generative evaluation (e.g., judge-based TruthfulQA) is reported for LLMs.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Sec. 4.1 states k=3 for all LLM experiments, but Fig. 6 shows the optimum at k=5 for Qwen; Table 8 reports IG average 59.75 while Table 1 reports 59.76; the λ ablation (Fig. 5) shows Qwen accuracy still rising at λ=10, suggesting results may be sensitive to under-explored hyperparameter ranges.

Baseline fairness is questionable in places: hyperparameters for baselines are taken from original papers or tuned on a held-out set, but steering strength λ for GRAINS is tuned per model/dataset, and the paper acknowledges RepE and ITI were excluded based on secondhand claims from other papers rather than direct comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper states code 'will be made publicly accessible' but provides no link or anonymized repository; given the many hyperparameters (k, λ, IG steps, number of steering samples, PCA choice) and small-sample construction (50 examples), the absence of released code is a real barrier to verification.

The technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially IG attribution (standard) + masking-based contrastive activations (close to CAA/contrastive explanation traditions) + PC1 aggregation (standard), combined with known intervention practices (additive injection, norm rescaling). The contribution is an empirical system rather than a new insight, so the evidence quality bar for a main-conference claim of SOTA steering is high—and it is only partially met.

Missing standard general-capability checks for LLMs beyond MMLU (e.g., GSM8K, open-ended fluency), and the GSM8K-style claim in the abstract only covers hallucination/alignment; some capability results (e.g., MMMU drops of ~1.5–2.6 points for GRAINS in Tables 3–4) are presented as 'only slightly below base' without significance analysis.

Some supporting evidence is thin or anecdotal: the qualitative analysis (Figs. 4, 7) shows cherry-picked examples; the modality-distribution analysis (Table 12) is on a single dataset; and the 'failure cases' discussion is speculative without quantification of undercorrection rates.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: using contrastive Integrated Gradients to identify influential tokens and construct layer-wise steering vectors is a sensible way to make inference-time steering token- and modality-aware, and the paper convincingly positions this against global-vector methods (CAA, ICV) and modality-specific methods (VTI, ICT).

Broad empirical coverage: two LLMs and three VLMs, three LLM safety benchmarks plus MMHal-Bench and SPA-VL, with strong baselines including LoRA fine-tuning and recent steering methods, and fair use of the same steering-construction samples for all baselines.

Extensive and informative ablations: attribution method (IG vs. SmoothGrad, vanilla gradients, random), token count k, PCA vs. mean aggregation, last-token vs. all-token injection, layer choice, preference loss vs. likelihood objective, and the norm-preservation step — each ablation is tied to a concrete design decision.

Strong capability-preservation analysis: the paper does not only report targeted gains but also shows MMLU/MMMU retention, generation-quality (BLEU accuracy) checks, cross-dataset generalization (Toxigen→RTP, MMHal→POPE), and a 72B-scale result, addressing the common failure mode of steering methods degrading general abilities.
Discussion of computational overhead is concrete (one-time ~96s/302s construction cost, <5% inference throughput drop), which supports the practicality claim.
Honest limitations section covering attribution quality, compute cost of gradient access, and the lack of formal guarantees.
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing or variance reporting. Results are single runs on relatively small test sets (e.g., 50 steering samples, dev/test splits of modest size), and several claimed margins (e.g., 0.44-point and 0.53-point IG ablation gains in Fig. 3, ~1-point differences between GRAINS and CAA in Table 1) are small enough that seed/sample variance could matter.

Some numerical inconsistencies across tables undermine confidence: the SPA-VL base LLaVA score is 40.24 in Table 2 but 42.38 in Table 4, and the paper describes Table 3/Table 4 'BLEU accuracy' while tabulating what appear to be different quantities; these need reconciliation.

The main results evaluate steering vectors built and tested on the same dataset (in-distribution). The cross-dataset experiments in Section 5.3 partially mitigate this, but headline claims would be stronger if generalization results were treated as central rather than supplementary.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: optimal λ differs substantially across models (peaking at 6 for Llama, 10+ for Qwen), and λ is tuned on a dev set; the paper acknowledges undercorrection from a mismatch between tuned global λ and instance-specific needs, but this limits the turnkey applicability claim.
The code footnote ('Code:') is empty, so reproducibility currently rests on the described hyperparameters and prompts alone; releasing code is essential for the claims to be independently verified.

The core mechanism is an incremental combination of known components (IG attribution, contrastive activation differences à la CAA, PCA aggregation, norm-preserving injection). The novelty lies mainly in the attribution-based token selection and its application to VLMs; the paper should sharpen the conceptual delta over CAA beyond token selection.

Multiple-choice accuracy on TruthfulQA and Toxigen is a coarse proxy; open-ended evaluations with human or stronger automatic judging are used only for MMHal, so gains on the LLM side could partly reflect formatting/probability biases.
